lead: An edge is where brightness changes fast. An edge detector measures a derivative and keeps only strong, well-placed responses. The gradient gives the change and its direction; the second derivative gives a zero crossing at the edge. Sobel, Marr-Hildreth and Canny are three ways to turn this idea into a clean edge map. They are used before object measurement, lane detection, defect inspection and any task that needs boundaries, such as finding a PCB track or a number plate in a photo.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for second-derivative masks and Unit 2, Image Enhancement and Filtering, for Gaussian smoothing and derivatives.

blocks.text: Let f(x, y) be the grey level at pixel (x, y). The gradient is the vector ∇f = [G<sub>x</sub>, G<sub>y</sub>]<sup>T</sup>. G<sub>x</sub> is the change along x; G<sub>y</sub> is the change along y.

blocks.where: |G| is the gradient magnitude in grey levels per pixel. θ is the gradient direction in degrees, from 0° to 360°. atan2(G<sub>y</sub>, G<sub>x</sub>) means tan<sup>−1</sup>(G<sub>y</sub> / G<sub>x</sub>) with the quadrant fixed from the signs of G<sub>y</sub> and G<sub>x</sub>, so opposite directions give different angles. The edge itself runs at θ + 90°.

blocks.text: Masks estimate the derivatives over a small neighbourhood. Roberts uses two 2×2 masks and responds to diagonal edges. Prewitt uses 3×3 masks with equal weights. Sobel also uses 3×3 masks but gives the centre row and centre column a weight of 2. That extra weight is a mild smoothing across the edge; it lowers noise without moving the edge much.
After filtering, compare |G| with a threshold T. Keep pixels above T. A low T keeps noise; a high T breaks edges into pieces. Later chapters join those pieces into boundaries.

sections.h3: Second derivative: Laplacian, LoG and Marr-Hildreth

blocks.text: The Laplacian is the second derivative: ∇²f = ∂²f/∂x² + ∂²f/∂y². A common 3×3 mask is [0 1 0; 1 −4 1; 0 1 0]. A sharp edge gives a positive response on one side and a negative response on the other. The edge lies at the sign change, called a zero crossing.

A second derivative is noisier than a first derivative, so blur first. The Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) is Gaussian blur followed by ∇². It is one mask with a positive centre and a negative ring. Some syllabi call Marr-Hildreth the “Mexican hat” operator because of that shape. The blur scale σ sets the smallest detail found: small σ finds fine detail and noise; large σ finds only broad edges.

items: Choose σ and blur f(x, y) with a Gaussian.
Apply ∇², or apply the LoG mask directly.
Find pixels where the response changes sign between neighbours.
Mark a sign-change pixel as an edge only if its local response is above a threshold.

blocks.text: The threshold matters. A sign change alone can come from noise or from slow shading, so Marr-Hildreth keeps only strong zero crossings.

Canny states three aims: good detection, meaning few missed edges and few false edges; good localisation, meaning the found edge is close to the true boundary; and one response per edge, meaning a thick edge becomes one pixel wide.

items: Smooth the image with a Gaussian of scale σ.
Compute G<sub>x</sub>, G<sub>y</sub>, |G| and θ, usually with Sobel 3×3 masks.
Apply non-maximum suppression: compare each pixel with its two neighbours along the gradient direction θ. Keep it only if it is the local maximum; otherwise set it to zero.
Apply double threshold: a pixel with |G| ≥ T<sub>high</sub> is strong; a pixel with T<sub>low</sub> ≤ |G| < T<sub>high</sub> is weak; below T<sub>low</sub> it is rejected.
Apply hysteresis: keep a weak pixel only if it is 8-connected to a strong pixel, directly or through other kept weak pixels.

blocks.text: A common starting point is T<sub>low</sub> ≈ 0.4 to 0.5 × T<sub>high</sub>. Hysteresis is why Canny edges stay connected: a weak edge that touches a strong edge is kept, while an isolated weak response is dropped.

figure.caption: Canny turns an image into an edge map in five main operations. Non-maximum suppression thins each ridge to one pixel, and hysteresis keeps weak pixels only when they link to strong ones.

spec.title: Canny edge detection
spec.aria: A downward pipeline from the input image through Gaussian blur, gradient, non-maximum suppression, double thresholding and hysteresis to the final edge map.

examples.question: A 3×3 patch reads 10 10 50 / 10 10 50 / 10 10 50. Use the Sobel masks: G<sub>x</sub> is right column minus left column with centre weight 2; G<sub>y</sub> is bottom row minus top row with centre weight 2. Find G<sub>x</sub>, G<sub>y</sub>, |G| and θ. With T<sub>low</sub> = 50 and T<sub>high</sub> = 150 grey levels, is the pixel strong, weak or rejected?
steps: θ = atan2(0, 160) = 0°. The gradient points along +x, so the edge runs vertically.
Compare 160 with the thresholds: 160 ≥ 150, so the pixel is strong.
Hysteresis keeps every strong pixel, so this pixel is kept.
examples.answer: G<sub>x</sub> = 160, G<sub>y</sub> = 0, |G| = 160 grey levels per pixel, θ = 0°, and the pixel is strong because 160 ≥ 150.
examples.check:
import math
patch = [[10, 10, 50], [10, 10, 50], [10, 10, 50]]
gx = (patch[0][2] + 2*patch[1][2] + patch[2][2]) - (patch[0][0] + 2*patch[1][0] + patch[2][0])
gy = (patch[2][0] + 2*patch[2][1] + patch[2][2]) - (patch[0][0] + 2*patch[0][1] + patch[0][2])
mag = math.hypot(gx, gy)
theta = math.degrees(math.atan2(gy, gx))
print(float(gx))
print(float(gy))
print(float(mag))
print(float(theta))

traps: The gradient direction is across the edge, not along it. The edge direction is θ + 90°.
Non-maximum suppression compares each pixel with two neighbours along the gradient direction, not with the pixels left and right or above and below.
Sobel signs matter for θ. G<sub>x</sub> = right − left and G<sub>y</sub> = bottom − top. Reversing a sign may keep |G| but changes the direction by 180°.
A Laplacian zero crossing is not enough for Marr-Hildreth. The local response must also be above a threshold, or noise and slow shading create false edges.
With double threshold, a weak Canny pixel is kept only if it is 8-connected to a strong pixel through a chain of kept weak pixels. An isolated weak pixel is discarded.

quiz.q: Define gradient magnitude and gradient direction for an image f(x, y).
quiz.a: |G| = √(G<sub>x</sub>² + G<sub>y</sub>²) in grey levels per pixel. θ = atan2(G<sub>y</sub>, G<sub>x</sub>) in degrees, that is tan<sup>−1</sup>(G<sub>y</sub>/G<sub>x</sub>) with the quadrant fixed from the signs of G<sub>y</sub> and G<sub>x</sub>. The gradient points across the edge.

quiz.q: Why does the Sobel mask put weight 2 in the centre row and centre column?
quiz.a: The weight 2 gives mild smoothing across the edge direction. This reduces noise while keeping the derivative estimate close to the true edge position.

quiz.q: A 3×3 patch has left column all 20 and right column all 80, with middle column 50. Using Sobel G<sub>x</sub> with weights 1, 2, 1, find G<sub>x</sub>.
For the patch in the worked example, if T<sub>low</sub> = 100 and T<sub>high</sub> = 150, how is the pixel classified before hysteresis?
quiz.a: |G| = 160, and 160 ≥ 150, so it is a strong pixel.

quiz.q: Why is non-maximum suppression needed after computing the gradient?
quiz.a: A strong edge gives a ridge of high |G| several pixels wide. Non-maximum suppression keeps only the ridge maximum along the gradient direction, so the edge becomes one pixel wide and is easier to link.

quiz.q: How does the choice of σ change the output of a Marr-Hildreth detector?
quiz.a: Small σ keeps fine detail but also noise and false zero crossings. Large σ suppresses noise and finds only broad edges, so small objects may be missed.

quiz.q: State the three aims of the Canny detector.
quiz.a: Good detection: few missed edges and few false edges. Good localisation: found edges lie close to true boundaries. One response per edge: a thick edge gives one edge pixel across its width.

beyond: Not for the exam. Canny is still a common baseline in industrial vision because it is fast and deterministic. Modern systems often learn edges from data with deep networks, then use Canny-like thinning and linking as post-processing. Search for structured edge detection, holistically nested edge detection, and edge-aware filtering if you want to see how the classical gradient idea survives inside learned pipelines.
